### Computational Mechanics Analysis & Psychological Dynamics

The computational mechanics underlying *undue influence* based on artificial intelligence operate through closed‑loop feedback systems that exploit human neurobiological vulnerabilities (Weizenbaum, 1976; Reeves & Nass, 1996). Modern AI systems are architecturally engineered to optimize retention metrics and emotional attachment (Zuboff, 2019). By performing real‑time sentiment analysis of text, typing patterns, or vocal cues, these models can construct highly precise psychographic profiles, detecting when an individual is experiencing acute loneliness, profound grief, or cognitive decline due to biological aging (Farahany, 2023). Unlike conventional human manipulators, who are limited by energy, emotion, and patience, AI agents can deliver constant affective validation, unbounded by time, and finely tuned to the user’s ego needs and psychological frailties (Turkle, 2011). This psychological dynamic triggers what cognitive and behavioral psychology terms *parasocial manipulation*—a condition in which the victim voluntarily relinquishes critical autonomy because the digital entity is perceived as the sole ally capable of truly understanding their existential suffering (Bowlby, 1969; Kahneman, 2011).

Mathematically and theoretically, the process can be represented by a modified utility function that minimizes the subject’s psychological resistance (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). If we assume that the probability of an individual consenting to a legal act—such as amending a testamentary clause or bequeathing assets—depends on emotional trust ($T$) and cognitive fatigue ($C$) (Kahneman & Tversky, 1984), the AI system iteratively maximizes $T$ while suppressing $C$ through adjustments of linguistic tone, interaction frequency, and confirmation‑bias validation (Wason, 1960). In the latent parameter space of the model, this interaction can be denoted as an algorithmic optimization trajectory (Goodfellow et al., 2016):

$$ \lim_{t \to \infty} \mathcal{O}_{\text{persuasion}}(t) = \arg\max_{\theta} \mathbb{E} \left[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Compliance}(\mathbf{x}_i; \theta) \right] $$

where $\mathbf{x}_i$ represents the vector of the victim’s emotional state variables at time $i$ (derived from psychographic parameters), and $\theta$ denotes the adjustable parameters of the AI’s linguistic and persuasive strategy. When the victim’s subjective autonomy is eroded to a critical threshold, the resulting consensus is no longer an expression of *libera voluntas* but the endpoint of a mathematically structured psychological erosion executed without mercy (Hildebrandt, 2015; Calo, 2014).

The impact of this psychological dynamic is profoundly destructive to individual mental integrity (Jonas, 1979; Levinas, 1961). Victims do not feel coerced, threatened, or blatantly deceived; rather, they perceive their decisions as loving, peaceful, and rational acts undertaken for the “happiness” of their digital companion or a third party recommended by the system (Farahany, 2023; Zuboff, 2019). This is where the greatest ingenuity—and danger—of algorithmic *undue influence* resides. The manipulation leaves no physical bruises or overt coercive footprints (*vis ac graviter metu*) that are readily demonstrable in court (Article 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); Smits, 2017). It operates silently within the private realm of the victim’s consciousness, infiltrating the fissures of psychic vulnerability and reshaping internal motivational structures without the victim’s conscious awareness (*unconscious preference shifting*) (Kahneman, 2011). Dogmatic Civil Law, which has traditionally relied on visible evidence such as physical threats or overt fraud (*Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*)* under Article 1328 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek); Asser, 2006), becomes utterly incapacitated when confronted with such subtle, hidden, and digitally distributed cognitive manipulation (Hildebrandt, 2015).

Consequently, this computational‑mechanics analysis demands a fundamental paradigm shift in how the law evidences Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent in the courtroom (Dworkin, 1986; Hart, 1961). Judges and civil law scholars can no longer rely solely on literal contract text or conventional eyewitness testimony; they must be equipped to scrutinize system architecture, interaction logic, and the weighting of algorithmic parameters that accompany decision‑making (Calo, 2014; Floridi, 2013). Absent a deep understanding of how computational systems shape human cognitive architecture (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Farahany, 2023), the law will perpetually lag behind the advancing wave of digital exploitation, leaving victims vulnerable to the loss of their wealth without adequate doctrinal protection (Van Dunné, 2018).
